question: The nurse is preparing to administer a schedule II injectable drug and is drawing up half of the contents of a single-use vial. Which nursing action is correct?
op_a: Ask another nurse to observe and cosign wasting the remaining drug from the vial.
op_b: Keep the remaining amount in the patients drawer to give at the next dose.
op_c: Record the amount unused in the patients medication record.
op_d: Dispose of the vial with the remaining drug into a locked collection box.
exp: Schedule II drugs are controlled substances, and all must be accounted for. When wasting a portion of a drug, another nurse should observe and cosign that a drug was wasted.

question: A patient is prescribed a medication and asks the nurse if the drug is available in a generic form. The nurse understands that a generic medication will have a name that
op_a: is a registered trademark.
op_b: is always capitalized.
op_c: describes the drugs chemical structure.
op_d: is non-proprietary.
exp: The generic name is the official, non-proprietary name for a drug. The brand name is the trademark name and is always capitalized. The chemical name describes the chemical structure of the drug.

question: A patient receives a prescription on which the provider has noted that a generic medication may be given. The patient asks the nurse what this means. What will the nurse tell the patient about generic drugs?
op_a: They contain the same inert ingredients as brand-name drugs.
op_b: They have chemical structures that are identical to proprietary drugs.
op_c: They tend to be less expensive than brand-name drugs.
op_d: They undergo extensive testing before they are marketed.
exp: Generic drugs are approved by the FDA if they are proved to be bioequivalent to the brand-name drug. They tend to be less expensive because manufacturers of these drugs do not have to do the extensive testing required of brand-name drugs before marketing. They are not identical to brand-name drugs and often have different inert ingredients.

question: The nurse reviews information about a drug and notes the initials USP after the drug's official name. The nurse understands that this designation indicates the drug
op_a: is a controlled substance.
op_b: is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
op_c: is available in generic form.
op_d: meets quality and safety standards.
exp: The USP designation is given to drugs that have met high standards for therapeutic use, patient safety, quality, purity, strength, packaging safety, and dosage form by the United States Pharmacopoeia National Formulary. The FDA classifies controlled substances with Roman numerals from I to V. The USP designation does not indicate FDA approval. The USP designation does not indicate generic availability.

question: The nurse is preparing to give a medication to a child. The child's parent asks whether the drug is safe for children. How will the nurse respond to the parent?
op_a: Drugs are tested on adults and safe doses for children are based on weights compared to adult weights.
op_b: Drugs are deemed safe for children over time when repeated use proves effectiveness and safety.
op_c: Drugs are tested for both efficacy and safety in children in order to be marketed for pediatric use.
op_d: Drugs are tested on children in postmarketing studies and on a limited basis.
exp: The Pediatric Research Equity Act requires drug manufacturers to test drugs on children.

question: Which law(s) govern all drug administration by nurses?
op_a: Drug Regulation and Reform Act
op_b: FDA Amendments Act
op_c: Nurse Practice Acts
op_d: The Controlled Substances Act
exp: Each state's Nurse Practice Act identifies how nurses administer medications. The other acts govern how drugs are marketed and tested.

question: The nurse administers a drug and miscalculates the dose by placing the decimal place one space to the right, resulting in a 10-fold overdose and the death of the patient. What offense does this represent?
op_a: Malfeasance
op_b: Malpractice
op_c: Misfeasance
op_d: Nonfeasance
exp: Misfeasance is negligence in giving either the wrong drug or the wrong dose, resulting in the death of the patient.

question: The nurse is busy and neglects to give a drug to a patient resulting in the patient's death. What offense does this represent?
op_a: Malfeasance
op_b: Malpractice
op_c: Misfeasance
op_d: Nonfeasance
exp: Nonfeasance is omitting a drug dose, resulting in the patient's death.

question: A patient is taking methadone as part of a heroin withdrawal program. The nurse understands that, in this instance, methadone is classified as which drug schedule?
op_a: C-I
op_b: C-II
op_c: C-III
op_d: C-V
exp: Methadone is a category II drug, with a high potential for drug abuse.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer a combination drug containing acetaminophen and codeine. The nurse knows that this drug is classified as which drug schedule?
op_a: C-II
op_b: C-III
op_c: C-IV
op_d: C-V
exp: Codeine is normally a category II drug, except when it is part of a combination product such as with acetaminophen, making it a category III drug.

question: The nurse is obtaining consent from a subject newly recruited for a clinical drug trial that will last for 6 months. All subjects will be given gift certificates for participating. One subject says, Well, I guess if the drug doesn't work, I'll just have to put up with the symptoms for 6 months. What will the nurse tell the subject?
op_a: Participation for the duration of the study is required.
op_b: Participation may end at any time without penalty.
op_c: Withdrawal from the study may end at any time, but the gift certificate will not be given.
op_d: You can request placement in the treatment group.
exp: All participants have the right to autonomy, which is the right to self-determination. Patients have the right to refuse to participate or to withdraw from a study at any time without penalty. Patients generally are not allowed to choose participation in either the treatment or the control group.

question: The nurse is assisting with a clinical drug trial in which the side effects of two effective drugs are being compared. A patient who would benefit from either drug has elected to withdraw from the study, and the nurse assists with the paperwork to facilitate this. This is an example of
op_a: autonomy.
op_b: beneficence.
op_c: justice.
op_d: veracity.
exp: All participants have the right to autonomy, which is the right to self-determination. Patients have the right to refuse to participate or to withdraw from a study at any time without penalty even if the health care provider disagrees with that choice.

question: During a clinical drug trial for a new medication, researchers note a previously unknown serious adverse effect occurring in more than 50% of subjects. The study is discontinued. Which ethical principle is being exercised?
op_a: Beneficence
op_b: Justice
op_c: Respect for persons
op_d: Veracity
exp: Beneficence is the duty to do good and to not harm others. Once a serious adverse effect is noted in a majority of subjects, researchers have an ethical obligation to stop the study.

question: In a 5-year experimental clinical trial to investigate a new cancer treatment, researchers in the second year note overwhelming improvement in almost all of the subjects in the treatment group. The lead researcher elects to continue the study. Which ethical principle is being violated?
op_a: Beneficence
op_b: Justice
op_c: Respect for persons
op_d: Veracity
exp: The principle of justice requires that all people be treated fairly, including equal access to health care for all. Once a benefit is demonstrated, it should be available to all participants.

question: The nurse is enrolling subjects for a double-blind experimental study. One patient asks the nurse to explain the role of the experimental group. The nurse will explain that subjects in the experimental group in this type of study
op_a: are selected for participation in that group.
op_b: have unique baseline characteristics.
op_c: receive a placebo.
op_d: receive the treatment being evaluated.
exp: In a double-blind experimental study, subjects in the experimental group receive the treatment or drug under study. They are randomly assigned and not selected. They should have similar baseline characteristics to those in the control group. They do not receive a placebo.

question: The nurse is obtaining signatures on consent forms for participation in a clinical drug trial. One patient says, Im not sure I want to do this, but I need the cash. The nurse will take which action?
op_a: Ask the patient to clarify concerns.
op_b: Reinforce that cash is given to all subjects equally.
op_c: Report this statement to the party named on the consent.
op_d: Review the elements of the study and obtain consent.
exp: If a nurse suspects that a patient is being coerced to participate in the study, the nurse should report this to the party named on the informed consent. When a patient verbalizes participation based on a financial reward, there is an element of coercion.

question: Which is characteristic of preclinical in vivo testing?
op_a: A comparison of experimental and control data in animals
op_b: A study conducted in a test tube in a laboratory
op_c: A study that determines the parameters of safe therapeutic doses
op_d: A study to assess the seriousness of the disease to be treated
exp: Preclinical in vivo testing is performed in animals or other living organisms. In vitro studies occur in test tubes. Safe therapeutic dose studies are part of clinical research. Prior to clinical trials, an assessment is made of the disease and its seriousness.

question: Many drugs marketed in the 1980s may not be effective in a majority of the population. The nurse understands that this is because these drugs
op_a: did not pass through the appropriate phases of clinical trials.
op_b: did not require human subject protections and are invalid.
op_c: were not tested on women, minorities, or children.
op_d: were tested on healthy subjects only.
exp: Drug research was historically done only with white males, causing uncertainty as to the validity of the research results.

question: The nurse is assisting with data collection in a study of drug effects in healthy subjects. The nurse assists with blood and urine collection to determine serum drug levels and the presence of metabolites in the urine. Which phase of a drug study does this represent?
op_a: Phase I
op_b: Phase II
op_c: Phase III
op_d: Phase IV
exp: Phase I drug trials are performed to assess safety and to identify the pharmacokinetics, such as metabolism and elimination, of drugs in healthy subjects.

question: The nurse is enrolling subjects for a clinical drug trial in which subjects will be randomly assigned to either a treatment or a placebo group. The pills in both groups will be in identical packaging with identical appearance. This is an example of which type of study?
op_a: Crossover
op_b: Double-blind
op_c: Open-label
op_d: Single-blind
exp: In a double-blind study, neither the subject nor the health care provider knows which group the subjects are in. Since there is no difference in the appearance or packaging of the pills, the health care providers will not be aware of which subjects receive the experimental drug and which ones receive the placebo.

question: The nurse is assisting with a clinical drug trial to test the safe dose of an analgesic medication and learns that subjects have been told that the study is about measuring the analgesic effects. Which ethical principle has been violated?
op_a: Beneficence
op_b: Justice
op_c: Respect for persons
op_d: Veracity
exp: Veracity requires health care professionals to tell the truth.

question: The nurse is participating in a clinical study of the effects of teaching on drug compliance. The subjects are randomly assigned to either an experimental group or a control group. Health professionals deliver one of two teaching modules to each patient. This is an example of which kind of study?
op_a: Double-blind
op_b: Open-label
op_c: Single-blind
op_d: Triple-blind
exp: In a single-blind study, only the subjects do not know which group they are assigned to.

question: A clinical drug trial is concluding a study of pharmacokinetics and safety of a drug in healthy individuals. The nurse will assist enrollment of participants into the next phase of the study and will include which subjects?
op_a: Healthy subjects
op_b: Healthy and ill subjects
op_c: Subjects with the disease the drug will treat
op_d: Subjects with other diseases
exp: After Phase I studies demonstrating drug safety and pharmacokinetics have been completed, the drug is tested on subjects who have the disease the drug will treat.

question: Before marketing a new drug that has been approved for use based on clinical effectiveness and safety, the manufacturer wishes to study the potential new uses for the drug. This is an example of which phase of study?
op_a: Phase I
op_b: Phase II
op_c: Phase III
op_d: Phase IV
exp: Phase IV studies are performed to examine potential new indications for approved drugs.

question: The nurse is participating in a clinical drug trial comparing two drugs for migraine headaches. Each group is randomly assigned to either drug A or drug B and then switched to the other drug group before being asked to compare the effects. This is an example of which type of study?
op_a: Crossover design
op_b: Double-blind experimental design
op_c: Matched pair design
op_d: Quasi-experimental design
exp: A crossover design uses each subject in several different situations. In this case, subjects receive both drugs and then compare the effects.

question: Which statement about the safety and efficacy of medications in children is accurate?
op_a: Children cannot give consent, so clinical drug trials are not performed on children.
op_b: Children can only be subjects in quasi-experimental clinical studies.
op_c: Data from adult clinical drug trials can be extrapolated to children.
op_d: Federal law requires that drugs for children be tested on children.
exp: The FDA Modernization Act of 1997 requires that drugs intended for use in children be tested on children.

question: Which are responsibilities of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)? (Select all that apply.)
op_a: To ensure a drug has accurate labeling
op_b: To ensure a drug is affordable
op_c: To ensure a drug is effective
op_d: To ensure a drug is free from adverse reactions
op_e: To ensure a drug is tested for harmful effects
exp: The FDA ensures that drugs are labeled correctly, that they are tested and proven effective for the conditions they are marketed to treat, and that they are tested for harmful effects. The FDA does not ensure affordability or freedom from adverse reactions, although these must be noted in drug information materials.

question: Which drugs will go through a pharmaceutic phase after it is administered?
op_a: Intramuscular cephalosporins
op_b: Intravenous vasopressors
op_c: Oral analgesics
op_d: Subcutaneous antiglycemics
exp: When drugs are administered parenterally, there is no pharmaceutic phase, which occurs when a drug becomes a solution that can cross the biologic membrane.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer an oral medication and wants to ensure a rapid drug action. Which form of the medication will the nurse administer?
op_a: Capsule
op_b: Enteric-coated pill
op_c: Liquid suspension
op_d: Tablet
exp: Liquid drugs are already in solution, which is the form necessary for absorption in the GI tract. The other forms must disintegrate into small particles and then dissolve before being absorbed.

question: The nurse is teaching a patient who will be discharged home with a prescription for an enteric-coated tablet. Which statement by the patient indicates understanding of the teaching?
op_a: I may crush the tablet and put it in applesauce to improve absorption.
op_b: I should consume acidic foods to enhance absorption of this medication.
op_c: I should expect a delay in onset of the drug's effects after taking the tablet.
op_d: I should take this medication with high-fat foods to improve its action.
exp: Enteric-coated tablets resist disintegration in the acidic environment of the stomach and disintegrate when they reach the small intestine. There is usually some delay in onset of actions after taking these medications. Enteric-coated tablets should not be crushed or chewed, which would alter the time and location of absorption. Acidic foods will not enhance the absorption of the medication. The patient should not eat high-fat food before ingesting an enteric-coated tablet, because high-fat foods decrease the absorption rate.

question: A patient who is newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus asks why insulin must be given by subcutaneous injection instead of by mouth. The nurse will explain that this is because
op_a: absorption is diminished by the first-pass effects in the liver.
op_b: absorption is faster when insulin is given subcutaneously.
op_c: digestive enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract prevent absorption.
op_d: the oral form is less predictable with more adverse effects.
exp: Insulin, growth hormones, and other protein-based drugs are destroyed in the small intestine by digestive enzymes and must be given parenterally. Because insulin is destroyed by digestive enzymes, it would not make it to the liver for metabolism with a first-pass effect. Subcutaneous tissue has fewer blood vessels, so absorption is slower in such tissue. Insulin is given subcutaneously because it is desirable to have it absorb slowly.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer an oral medication that is water-soluble. The nurse understands that this drug
op_a: must be taken on an empty stomach.
op_b: requires active transport for absorption.
op_c: should be taken with fatty foods.
op_d: will readily diffuse into the gastrointestinal tract.
exp: Water-soluble drugs require a carrier enzyme or protein to pass through the GI membrane.

question: A nurse is preparing to administer an oral drug that is best absorbed in an acidic environment. How will the nurse give the drug?
op_a: On an empty stomach
op_b: With a full glass of water
op_c: With food
op_d: With high-fat food
exp: Food can stimulate the production of gastric acid so medications requiring an acidic environment should be given with a meal. High-fat foods are useful for drugs that are lipid soluble.

question: The nurse is preparing an injectable drug and wants to administer it for rapid absorption. How will the nurse give this medication?
op_a: IM into the deltoid muscle
op_b: IM into the gluteal muscle
op_c: SubQ into abdominal tissue
op_d: SubQ into the upper arm
exp: Drugs given IM are absorbed faster in muscles that have more blood vessels, such as the deltoid, rather than those with fewer blood vessels, such as the gluteals. Subcutaneous routes are used when absorption needs to be slower and more sustained.

question: The nurse is reviewing medication information with a nursing student prior to administering an oral drug and notes that the drug has extensive first-pass effects. Which statement by the student indicates a need for further teaching about this medication?
op_a: The first-pass effect means the drug may be absorbed into systemic circulation from the intestinal lumen.
op_b: The first-pass effect means the drug may be changed to an inactive form and excreted.
op_c: The first-pass effect means the drug may be changed to a metabolite, which may be more active than the original.
op_d: The first-pass effect means the drug may be unchanged as it passes through the liver.
exp: Drugs that undergo first-pass metabolism are absorbed into the portal vein from the intestinal lumen and go through the liver where they are either unchanged or are metabolized to an inactive or a more active form.

question: The nurse prepares to change a patient's medication from an intravenous to an oral form and notes that the oral form is ordered in a higher dose. The nurse understands that this is due to differences in
op_a: bioavailability.
op_b: pinocytosis.
op_c: protein binding.
op_d: tachyphylaxis.
exp: Oral drugs may have less bioavailability because a lower percentage of the drug reaches the systemic circulation. Pinocytosis refers to the process by which cells carry a solute across a membrane. Protein binding can occur with both routes. Tachyphylaxis describes a rapid decrease in response to drugs that occurs when tolerance develops quickly.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer a drug and learns that it binds to protein at a rate of 90%. The patient's serum albumin level is low. The nurse will observe the patient for
op_a: decreased drug absorption.
op_b: decreased drug interactions.
op_c: decreased drug toxicity.
op_d: increased drug effects.
exp: Drugs that are highly protein-bound bind with albumin and other proteins, leaving less free drug in circulation. If a patient has a low albumin, the drug is not bound, and there is more free drug to cause drug effects. There would be increased absorption, increased interactions with other drugs, and increased toxicity.

question: The nurse is administering two drugs to a patient and learns that both drugs are highly protein-bound. The nurse may expect
op_a: decreased bioavailability of both drugs.
op_b: decreased drug effects.
op_c: decreased drug interactions.
op_d: increased risk of adverse effects.
exp: Two drugs that are highly protein-bound will compete for protein-binding sites, leaving more free drug in circulation and an increased risk of adverse effects as well as increased bioavailability, increased drug effects, and increased drug interactions.

question: A patient has been taking a drug that has a protein-binding effect of 75%. The provider adds a new medication that has a protein-binding effect of 90%. The nurse will expect
op_a: decreased drug effects of the first drug.
op_b: decreased therapeutic range of the first drug.
op_c: increased drug effects of the first drug.
op_d: increased therapeutic range of the first drug.
exp: Adding another highly protein-bound drug will displace the first drug from protein-binding sites and release more free drug increasing the drug's effects. This does not alter the therapeutic range, which is the serum level between drug effectiveness and toxicity.

question: The nurse gives a medication to a patient with a history of liver disease. The nurse will monitor this patient for
op_a: decreased drug effects.
op_b: increased drug effects.
op_c: decreased therapeutic range.
op_d: increased therapeutic range.
exp: Liver diseases such as cirrhosis and hepatitis alter drug metabolism by inhibiting the drug-metabolizing enzymes in the liver. When the drug metabolism rate is decreased, excess drug accumulation can occur and lead to toxicity.

question: The nurse gives 800 mg of a drug that has a half-life of 8 hours. How much drug will be left in the body in 24 hours if no additional drug is given?
op_a: None
op_b: 50 mg
op_c: 100 mg
op_d: 200 mg
exp: Eight hours after the drug is given, there will be 400 mg left. Eight hours after that (16 hours), there will be 200 mg left. At 24 hours, there will be 100 mg left.

question: If a drug has a half-life of 12 hours and is given twice daily starting at 0800 on a Monday, when will a steady state be achieved?
op_a: 0800 on Tuesday
op_b: 0800 on Wednesday
op_c: 0800 on Thursday
op_d: 0800 on Friday
exp: Steady-state levels occur at 3 to 5 half-lives. Wednesday at 0800 is 4 half-lives from the original dose.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer a drug that is ordered to be given twice daily. The nurse reviews the medication information and learns that the drug has a half-life of 24 hours. What will the nurse do next?
op_a: Administer the medication as ordered.
op_b: Contact the provider to discuss daily dosing.
op_c: Discuss every-other-day dosing with the provider.
op_d: Hold the medication and notify the provider.
exp: A drug with a longer half-life should be given at longer intervals to avoid drug toxicity.

question: The nurse is caring for a patient who has taken an overdose of aspirin several hours prior. The provider orders sodium bicarbonate to be given. The nurse understands that this drug is given for which purpose?
op_a: To counter the toxic effects of the aspirin
op_b: To decrease the half-life of the aspirin
op_c: To increase the excretion of the aspirin
op_d: To neutralize the acid of the aspirin
exp: Aspirin is a weak acid and is more readily excreted in alkaline urine. Sodium bicarbonate alkalizes the urine. It does not act as an antidote to aspirin, decrease the half-life, or neutralize its pH.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer a drug that is eliminated through the kidneys. The nurse reviews the patient's chart and notes that the patient has increased serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). The nurse will perform which action?
op_a: Administer the drug as ordered.
op_b: Anticipate a shorter than usual half-life of the drug.
op_c: Expect decreased drug effects when the drug is given.
op_d: Notify the provider and discuss giving a lower dose.
exp: Increased creatinine and BUN indicate decreased renal function so a drug that is eliminated through the kidneys can become toxic. The nurse should discuss a lower dose with the provider. The drug will have a longer half-life and will exhibit increased effects with decreased renal function.

question: The nurse understands that the length of time needed for a drug to reach the minimum effective concentration (MEC) is the
op_a: duration of action.
op_b: onset of action.
op_c: peak action time.
op_d: time response curve.
exp: The onset of action is the time it takes to reach the MEC. Duration of action is the length of time a drug has a pharmacologic effect. Peak action time occurs when the drug reaches its highest blood level. The time response curve is an evaluation of the other three measures.

question: The nurse administers albuterol to a patient who has asthma. The albuterol acts by stimulating beta2- adrenergic receptors to cause bronchodilation. The nurse understands that albuterol is a beta-adrenergic
op_a: agonist.
op_b: antagonist.
op_c: inhibitor.
op_d: depressant.
exp: An agonist medication is one that stimulates a certain type of cell to produce a response.

question: The nurse is explaining to the patient why a nonspecific drug has so many side effects. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?
op_a: Nonspecific drugs can affect specific receptor types in different body tissues.
op_b: Nonspecific drugs can affect a variety of receptor types in similar body tissues.
op_c: Nonspecific drugs can affect hormone secretion as well as cellular functions.
op_d: Nonspecific drugs require higher doses than specific drugs to be effective.
exp: Nonspecific drugs can act on one type of receptor but in different body tissues, or a variety of receptor types, or act on hormones to produce effects. Nonspecific drugs do not require higher doses.

question: The nurse is preparing to give a dose of gentamicin to a patient and notes that the most recent serum gentamicin trough level was 2 mcg/mL. What will the nurse do next?
op_a: Administer the drug as ordered.
op_b: Administer the drug and monitor for adverse effects.
op_c: Notify the provider to discuss decreasing the dose.
op_d: Notify the provider to report a toxic drug level.
exp: The trough drug level for gentamicin should be less than 2 mcg/mL. The nurse should not administer the drug and should notify the provider of the toxic level.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer the first dose of digoxin (Lanoxin) to a patient and notes that the dose ordered is much higher than the usual recommended dose. Which action will the nurse perform?
op_a: Administer the dose as ordered.
op_b: Give the dose and monitor for toxicity.
op_c: Hold the dose until reviewing it with the provider.
op_d: Refuse to give the dose.
exp: Digoxin requires a loading dose when first prescribed.

question: The nurse administers a narcotic analgesic to a patient who has been receiving it for 1 day after orthopedic surgery. The patient reports no change in pain 30 minutes after the medication is given. The nurse recognizes that this patient is exhibiting
op_a: drug-seeking behavior.
op_b: drug tolerance.
op_c: the placebo effect.
op_d: tachyphylaxis.
exp: Tachyphylaxis is a rapid decrease in response, or acute tolerance. Tolerance to drug effects can occur with narcotics, requiring increased doses in order to achieve adequate drug effects. Nurses often mistake drug- seeking behavior for drug tolerance. The placebo effect occurs when the patient experiences a response with an inactive drug.

question: The nurse is performing a pain assessment on a patient of Asian descent. The patient does not describe the pain when asked to do so and looks away from the nurse. What will the nurse do next?
op_a: Ask the patient's family member to evaluate the patient's pain.
op_b: Conclude that the patient's pain is minimal.
op_c: Evaluate the patient's non-verbal pain cues.
op_d: Suspect that the patient is experiencing severe pain.
exp: Patients of Asian descent might speak in soft tones and avoid direct eye contact while being comfortable with long silences. It is not correct to ask family members to evaluate pain. Without assessment of non-verbal cues, the nurse cannot determine whether the pain is minimal or severe.

question: The nurse is preparing to discuss long-term care needs with a patient newly diagnosed with a chronic disease. The patient is of Latin American descent. The nurse will plan to take which action when teaching this patient?
op_a: Discussing long-term outcomes associated with compliance of the prescribed regimen
op_b: Highlighting various traditional healing practices that will not be effective for this patient's care
op_c: Providing factual information and answering all questions as they arise
op_d: Providing teaching in increments, allowing periods of silence to allow assimilation of information
exp: The nurse should provide factual information and answer questions. Persons of Latin American descent have less dependence on time schedules and do not tend to have a future orientation. They are not comfortable with periods of silence. Nurses should be receptive to traditional healing practices and seek ways to include those in care when they do not hinder safe and effective care; highlighting practices that won't work may convey a lack of respect for these traditions.

question: A Native American patient has just been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. The nurse preparing a teaching plan for this patient understands that which aspect of the disease and disease management may be most difficult for this patient?
op_a: Body image changes
op_b: Management of meal and medication schedules
op_c: Perception of the disease as punishment from God
op_d: The sense of dependence on others
exp: Non-European cultural groups such as those of Native American descent have less dependence on time schedules. Disease management will likely focus more on present concerns about alleviating current discomfort and less on measures to promote long-term wellness or treat a chronic illness.

question: A patient who is of Filipino descent is admitted to the hospital. The nurse goes to the room to start intravenous fluids and to perform an admission assessment and finds several family members in the room. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
op_a: Ask the family to wait in the hallway until the admission tasks are completed.
op_b: Determine which family member is the family patriarch and address questions to him.
op_c: Invite family members to assist with appropriate tasks during the admission process.
op_d: Provide chairs for family members and ask them to stay seated during the admission.
exp: In general, the Filipino culture expects that family members will stay at a patient's bedside and participate in his or her care. The nurse should include the family in appropriate tasks. It is not correct to ask the family to wait in the hall or to sit in chairs and not participate. Filipino families do not necessarily depend on family patriarchs.

question: The nurse is caring for a patient who is a member of the local Native American community. The patient is refusing medications and treatments in spite of repeated attempts to explain the importance of these interventions. Which is an appropriate nursing action?
op_a: Ask a family member about traditional healing practices that might be better accepted.
op_b: Enlist the help of a family member to explain the need for the medications and treatments.
op_c: Find a hospital staff member who is Native American to help provide teaching for this patient.
op_d: Suggest a Social Work consult to the patient's provider.
exp: Members of some cultures may use traditional healers, and this should be accommodated whenever possible. Showing respect for this patient's culture will help to establish trust and thus greater cooperation. It is important for the nurse not to make generalizations within and among cultural groups, so asking a family member to describe what this particular patient needs is the better choice. Finding a hospital staff member who is Native American assumes that all Native Americans have the same practices. Deferring to a Social Worker is not necessary. Enlisting a family member to explain the need for the medications is just another way of imposing treatments on this person without respecting their cultural needs.

question: The nurse is caring for an African-American patient who appears to understand instructions for self-care but does not carry out basic self-care tasks. The nurse understands that the patient may
op_a: be poorly educated and lack basic comprehension skills.
op_b: need more time and personal space to assimilate what is taught.
op_c: require the use of culturally appropriate words and phrases when teaching.
op_d: view illness as punishment and lack desire to change the outcome.
exp: African Americans may use a common style of speaking. This vernacular English may be quite different in some cases from standard English, so if things are misunderstood, it is possible that vernacular terminology may need to be used. This vernacular English does not mean that patients are poorly educated or uncommunicative. African Americans do not tend to need more space and do not necessarily view illness as punishment.

question: The nurse notes that a patient of African American descent who is taking an oral antihypertensive medication continues to have elevated blood pressure three months after beginning the medication regimen. The nurse suspects that the patient may be
op_a: consuming ethnic foods that interfere with absorption of the drug.
op_b: discarding the medication.
op_c: experiencing allergic reactions to the medication.
op_d: metabolizing the drug differently than expected.
exp: Certain classifications of medications have different effects in individuals whose genetic markers are predominantly characteristic of a certain biologic group. African Americans respond poorly to several classes of antihypertensive agents.

question: The nurse is caring for a postoperative patient who is of Asian descent. The patient reports little relief from pain even while taking an opioid analgesic containing codeine and acetaminophen. What does the nurse suspect that this patient is exhibiting?
op_a: Drug-seeking behavior
op_b: Heightened pain perception
op_c: Poor understanding of expected drug effects
op_d: Rapid metabolism of one of the drug's components
exp: Certain classifications of medications have different effects in individuals whose genetic markers are predominantly characteristic of a certain biologic group. Persons of Asian descent may have a decreased response to some drugs because they are more likely to have higher levels of CYP2D6 enzymes.

question: The nurse is caring for an African-American patient who is taking warfarin (Coumadin) to prevent blood clots. The nurse will monitor this patient carefully for which effect?
op_a: Decreased therapeutic effects
op_b: Heightened risk for hemorrhage
op_c: Increased risk of hypersensitivity
op_d: Potential risk of paradoxical effects
exp: Certain classifications of medications have different effects in individuals whose genetic markers are predominantly characteristic of a certain biologic group. African-American patients will tend to have a decreased therapeutic effect from warfarin (Coumadin).

question: A family member expresses concern that a patient is taking several herbal remedies and worries that they may be unsafe. The nurse will respond by saying that herbs
op_a: are classified as medications by the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994.
op_b: are regulated by the government and are determined to be safe.
op_c: aren't usually effective but are generally harmless.
op_d: should be discussed with the patient's provider in conjunction with other medications.
exp: Herbs are sometimes useful but can also be useless or dangerous. There are two types of monographs under development to compile information about these substances, but there are no agencies that regulate safety and efficacy. Patients should always tell providers if they are taking any herbal remedies since there are known drug-herbal interactions and side effects.

question: A pregnant woman tells the nurse that she is taking ginger to reduce morning sickness. What will the nurse tell this patient?
op_a: Ginger can cause fetal birth defects.
op_b: Ginger is not safe during pregnancy.
op_c: Ginger can cause abortion in low doses.
op_d: Ginger may be taken in low doses for up to 4 days.
exp: Ginger may be taken during pregnancy for morning sickness, but only on a short-term, low-dose basis. There is no indication that it causes fetal birth defects. Ginger is an abortifacient in large amounts.

question: A patient asks the nurse about an herbal supplement and reports that it has a USP seal of approval. The nurse explains that this indicates
op_a: identity, potency, purity, and labeling accuracy.
op_b: premarket testing for safety and efficacy.
op_c: structure and function claims may be made.
op_d: the supplement's ability to prevent and treat disease.
exp: The USP seal of approval is a fee-based test and reports on identity, potency, purity, and labeling accuracy. It does not indicate premarket research on safety and accuracy, does not allow manufacturers to make claims about the function of the products, and does not indicate the substance's ability to prevent and treat disease.

question: A woman reports using aloe vera to treat constipation. Which response by the nurse is correct?
op_a: Aloe vera is for external use only.
op_b: Please tell me if you are taking cardiac medications or diuretics.
op_c: Side effects of aloe vera are common.
op_d: You may experience a decrease in menstrual flow while taking aloe vera.
exp: Patients taking aloe vera should consult with their provider if taking cardiac medications or diuretics. It is for internal and external use. Side effects are rare except with long-term use or in large doses. Aloe vera can increase menstrual flow.

question: A woman who is experiencing hot flashes associated with menopause asks the nurse about using black cohosh. Which response by the nurse is correct?
op_a: Black cohosh may be used long term in place of hormone replacement therapy.
op_b: Black cohosh may contribute to iron toxicity.
op_c: Black cohosh may interact with antihypertensive drugs.
op_d: Black cohosh treats menopausal symptoms without altering hormone levels.
exp: Black cohosh may increase the action of antihypertensive medications. It should not be used longer than 6 months. It may decrease iron absorption, contributing to iron deficiency. Black cohosh suppresses luteinizing hormone and optimizes estrogen levels.

question: A patient who has HIV asks the nurse about taking echinacea to improve immune function. What will the nurse tell this patient?
op_a: The root extract is useful for treating upper respiratory and urinary tract infections.
op_b: This use is currently being studied in patients who have HIV.
op_c: Use it as needed when antibiotics fail to treat your infections.
op_d: You may use it safely up to 8 weeks at a time as a preventive medication.
exp: The use of echinacea to stimulate the immune system of patients with HIV is being investigated, but its use is currently not recommended.

question: The nurse is counseling a female patient who reports taking feverfew to treat premenstrual syndrome and migraines. Which statement by the patient indicates understanding of the teaching?
op_a: I should experience immediate effects with this herb.
op_b: I should not take feverfew if I get pregnant.
op_c: I should take feverfew with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to enhance its effects.
op_d: If I develop gastrointestinal (GI) upset, I should stop taking feverfew immediately.
exp: Feverfew should be avoided during pregnancy. Patients may not experience effects for 4 to 6 weeks. Patients should not take feverfew with NSAIDs without consulting the provider. Discontinuing feverfew abruptly can cause rebound headache.

question: The nurse is providing preoperative education to a patient who will have surgery in several weeks. The patient denies taking anticoagulant medications but reports using herbal supplements. Which herb would cause the nurse to be concerned?
op_a: Echinacea
op_b: Ginkgo biloba
op_c: Kava
op_d: Sage
exp: Ginkgo can prolong bleeding time and therefore should be discontinued 2 weeks prior to surgery.

question: The nurse provides counseling to a patient who reports taking kava to treat anxiety-related symptoms. Which statement by the patient indicates understanding of the teaching?
op_a: I may take kava with lorazepam (Ativan).
op_b: I may develop a serious skin disorder while taking kava.
op_c: I should avoid alcohol while taking kava.
op_d: I should avoid St. Johns wort and valerian while taking kava.
exp: Kava can cause drowsiness and may cause liver damage. Patients should be cautioned against drinking alcohol while taking kava. Kava increases the effect of other benzodiazepines, so it should not be taken with lorazepam. It does not cause skin disorders. It may be taken with St. Johns wort and valerian.

question: The spouse of a patient who is an alcoholic asks the nurse about dietary supplements that may help prevent liver disease. Which herb will the nurse suggest the patient discuss with a provider who has prescriptive authority?
op_a: Ginkgo biloba
op_b: Kava
op_c: Milk thistle
op_d: Sage
exp: Milk thistle can prevent damage to liver cells and stimulates regeneration of liver cells.

question: A patient reports taking St. Johns wort to treat symptoms of depression and asks the nurse how to use this product safely and effectively. Which response by the nurse is correct?
op_a: Apply sunscreen while taking St. Johns wort.
op_b: It is safe to take St. Johns wort with prescription antidepressants.
op_c: St. Johns wort does not affect nutrition.
op_d: You should take St. Johns wort as needed when symptoms occur.
exp: St. Johns wort can cause photosensitivity, so patients should be counseled to use sunscreen. It should not be taken with prescription antidepressants because it increases the risk of suicidal ideation. It interferes with the absorption of iron and other minerals. Effects do not occur for 4 to 8 weeks, so it cannot be taken as needed.

question: A man is diagnosed with benign prostatic hypertrophy and wants to avoid surgery. He asks the nurse about using saw palmetto. What information will the nurse include when teaching this patient about this herb?
op_a: Gastric disturbances are common while using this herb.
op_b: Saw palmetto may help treat erectile dysfunction (ED) as well.
op_c: Use saw palmetto for up to 30 days and stop taking it when effects occur.
op_d: You should stop taking the herb 1 to 2 weeks prior to prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing.
exp: Saw palmetto can cause a false-negative test result for PSA, so patients should stop taking it 1 to 2 weeks prior to this test. GI effects are rare. It is not effective in treating ED. Effects usually dont occur until 30 days, and it may be taken long term.

question: A patient is taking valerian, or herbal valium, to induce sleep. What will the nurse teach this patient about this herb?
op_a: Habituation and addiction are likely.
op_b: Hangover effects are common with usual doses.
op_c: Liver function tests must be monitored with long-term use.
op_d: Valerian has a high risk for overdose.
exp: Liver function tests must be monitored with long-term use, and valerian should be discontinued if these are elevated. Habituation and addiction are rare. Hangover effects occur with high doses. There is no increased risk for overdose.

question: A patient asks the nurse about the safety of herbal products in general. Which response by the nurse is correct?
op_a: Consumers should research products and their manufacturers before taking.
op_b: Manufacturers are required to list interactions of herbs with drugs and food.
op_c: Products manufactured for drug and grocery store chains are safe.
op_d: Toxicological analysis is required of all commercial herbal products.
exp: There are no comprehensive regulations of herbal supplements regarding safety and efficacy, so consumers should research herbs and product manufacturers. Companies manufacturing for drug and grocery stores are suspect and do not always list all ingredients on their labels.

question: Which information can consumers expect to be included in labeling of herbal products?
op_a: Actions and uses
op_b: Interactions and precautions
op_c: Scientific name of the product
op_d: Safety and efficacy study results
exp: Manufacturers should list the scientific name of the product and the parts of the plant used in preparation. They are not required to list actions, uses, interactions, precautions, and any results of safety or efficacy studies.

question: Which herbal remedies are often used for gastrointestinal disorders? (Select all that apply.)
op_a: Chamomile
op_b: Cranberry
op_c: Dong quai
op_d: Echinacea
exp: Chamomile, ginger, and peppermint are often used to treat gastrointestinal disorders.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer a medication to a 6-month-old infant. The nurse will monitor closely for signs of drug toxicity based on the knowledge that, compared to adults, infants have a.
op_a: an increased percentage of total body fat.
op_b: immature hepatic and renal function.
op_c: more protein receptor sites.
op_d: more rapid gastrointestinal transit time.
exp: The liver and kidneys are the primary organs for metabolism and excretion and are immature in infants. This allows drugs to accumulate and increases the risk for drug toxicity. Infants have a lower proportion of body fat than adults and fewer protein receptors. They do have more rapid gastrointestinal transit time, but this decreases the amount of drug absorbed.

question: The nurse reviews information about a drug and learns that it is best absorbed in an acidic environment. When giving this drug to a 1-year-old patient, the nurse will expect to administer a dose that will be
op_a: equal to an adult dose.
op_b: less than an adult dose.
op_c: more than an adult dose.
op_d: twice the usual adult dose.
exp: Because the child's gastric pH is more alkaline than the adult's, less drug will be absorbed. Therefore, the dose should be increased.

question: The nurse assumes care for an infant who is showing signs of drug toxicity to a drug given several hours prior. The nurse checks the dose and confirms that the dose is consistent with standard dosing guidelines. Which characteristic of the drug will likely explain this response in this patient?
op_a: It is acidic.
op_b: It is highly protein-bound.
op_c: It is not fat-soluble.
op_d: It is water-soluble.
exp: With fewer protein-binding sites, there is more active drug available. This requires a reduction in the dose for infants. Drugs that are acidic are not as readily absorbed in infants, since their gastric pH tends to be more alkaline. Infants have a lower proportion of body fat; fat-soluble drugs would need to be decreased to prevent toxicity. Until about age 2 years of age, pediatric patients require larger than usual doses of water-soluble drugs to achieve therapeutic effects.

question: The parent is concerned about giving a child medication because of the lack of knowledge about the effects of drugs on children. The nurse discusses legislation passed in 2002 and 2003 about pediatric pharmacology. Which is true about these laws?
op_a: They forbid providers from prescribing medications unless they have been FDA-approved for use in children.
op_b: They mandate consistent, evidence-based dosing guidelines for use in children.
op_c: They provide federal grants to fund pediatric pharmaceutical research.
op_d: They require drug manufacturers to study pediatric medication use.
exp: In 2003, a law known as the Pediatric Research Equity Act joined the Best Pharmaceuticals Act of 2002 to require drug manufacturers to study pediatric medication use and offer incentives for pediatric pharmacology research. Providers are not forbidden to prescribe drugs in children that are not FDA-approved. The laws do not mandate the use of evidence-based guidelines and do not provide grants to fund research.

question: The nurse will administer an intravenous medication to an adolescent patient. When preparing the adolescent for the IV insertion, which is an appropriate action by the nurse?
op_a: Allowing the patient to verbalize concerns about the procedure
op_b: Covering the insertion site with a bandage after the procedure is completed
op_c: Explaining any possible adverse drug reactions
op_d: Reassuring the patient that only one body part will be used
exp: Allowing the adolescent to verbalize concerns about the medication and its regimen may offer opportunities to clarify misconceptions and teach new information. Preschool-age children may have concerns about harm to their body and need to have sites covered. Adolescents still have a present focus, so discussing future adverse reactions is not especially helpful. Preschool and school-age children fear bodily harm and require reassurance that only one body part will be affected.

question: An infant will receive a topical medication. What instruction will the nurse include when teaching the parents how to administer the medication?
op_a: Apply a thin layer to the affected area.
op_b: Apply liberally to the skin on and around the area.
op_c: Use the medication less frequently than what is recommended for adults.
op_d: Use the medication more frequently than what is recommended for adults.
exp: Topical medications may be altered by skin tissue condition. Children have thinner, more porous skin and have a proportionately higher skin surface area than adults and thus absorb topical medications more readily. Caregivers should be advised to use only a thin layer on the affected body part. This difference in skin does not affect the frequency of administering topical medications.

question: The provider has ordered that vitamin D drops be given to a newborn. Based on the knowledge of drug distribution in infants, the nurse understands that the infant may need
op_a: a higher dose.
op_b: a lower dose.
op_c: less frequent dosing.
op_d: more frequent dosing.
exp: Neonates and young infants tend to have less body fat than older children, meaning that they need less of fat-soluble medications since these medications won't be bound in fat tissue. Higher doses would lead to drug toxicity. Body fat does not affect the frequency of dosing.

question: The nurse is caring for a 5-year-old child. The child is taking a drug that has a known therapeutic range in adults, and the nurse checks that the ordered dose is correct and notes that the child's serum drug level is within normal limits. The child complains of a headache, which is a common sign of toxicity for this drug. Which action will the nurse take?
op_a: Administer the drug since the drug levels are normal.
op_b: Attribute the headache to non-drug causes.
op_c: Hold the next dose and contact the provider.
op_d: Request an order for an analgesic medication.
exp: The therapeutic ranges established for many drug levels are based on adult studies, so it is important for the nurse to assess pediatric patients in conjunction with monitoring drug levels. The nurse should notify the provider of the reaction. Because headaches are a symptom of toxicity for this drug, the nurse should not ignore the symptom.

question: The nurse is preparing to give a 7-year-old child a bitter-tasting oral medication. The child asks the nurse if the medicine tastes bad. To help the child take this medication, which action will the nurse take?
op_a: Allow the child to delay taking the medication until the parent arrives.
op_b: Enlist the assistance of other staff to help restrain the child.
op_c: Tell the child that it doesnt taste bad if it is swallowed quickly.
op_d: Tell the child that it tastes bad and offer a choice of beverages to drink afterwards.
exp: School-age children should be permitted more control, involvement in the process, and honest information. The nurse should tell the child the truth and offer the child a choice about what to drink to wash down the medicine. Medications must be given on schedule, so allowing the child a choice about when to take a medication is not acceptable. Restraining a child should not be used unless other methods have failed. Telling the child the medication doesnt taste bad is not honest and will reduce the child's trust in the nurse.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer an oral liquid medication to an 11-month-old child who is fussy and uncooperative. Which action will the nurse take to facilitate giving this medication?
op_a: Adding honey to the medication to improve the taste
op_b: Putting the medication in the infant's formula
op_c: Requesting an injectable form of the medication
op_d: Using a syringe and allowing the parent to give the medication
exp: When possible, family members or caregivers should be solicited to assist in medication administration. Infants should not receive honey because of the risk of botulism. A syringe allows more control over the amount of medication in the infant's mouth and should be used. Mixing the medication in a bottle requires ensuring that the infant takes the entire bottle in order to get the medication dose. Using an injectable form of medication is more traumatic and should be used only when an oral route is not possible or is contraindicated.

question: A 2-year-old child will receive several doses of an intramuscular medication. The nurse caring for this child will use which intervention to help the child cope with this regimen?
op_a: Allowing the child to give pretend shots to a doll with an empty syringe
op_b: Allowing the child to select a Band-Aid to wear after each medication is given
op_c: Ensuring privacy while giving the medication
op_d: Explaining that the medicine will help the child to feel better
exp: Simple explanations, a firm approach, and enlisting the imagination of a toddler through play may enhance cooperation. Allowing the child to practice on a doll may help the toddler tolerate the injections. Preschool and school-age children fear bodily injury, and Band-Aids are important with those age groups. Adolescents need privacy, and school-age children and adolescents can understand the use of a medication in relation to future outcomes.

question: A preschool-age child has moderate dehydration and needs a rapid bolus of fluids. To provide atraumatic care and administer fluids most effectively, what action will the nurse take?
op_a: Apply a eutectic mixture of local anesthetic (EMLA) just before inserting an intravenous line.
op_b: Ask the child's parents to restrain the child during venipuncture so fluids may be administered.
op_c: Request an order for nasogastric (NG) fluids to avoid the trauma of venipuncture.
op_d: Use a powdered lidocaine preparation prior to insertion of the intravenous needle.
exp: One method to ensure atraumatic care is through the use of topical analgesics before IV injections. Powdered lidocaine preparations are effective in reducing the pain and fear associated with invasive procedures, such as venipuncture. EMLA is useful only if applied 1 to 2.5 hours prior to IV insertion. Asking parents to restrain the child for a painful procedure can cause stress and anxiety for both the child and the parents. NG fluids are traumatic and are uncomfortable long past the insertion of the NG tube.

question: The nurse is preparing to administer an intramuscular medication to a 4-year-old child who starts to cry and screams, I dont want a shot! What is the nurse's next action?
op_a: Acknowledge that shots hurt and tell the child to be brave.
op_b: Engage the child in a conversation about preschool and favorite activities.
op_c: Enlist the assistance of another nurse to help restrain the child.
op_d: Explain to the child that it will only hurt for a few seconds.
exp: Distraction may be used for pain and anxiety control in this age group. Engaging the child in a conversation may distract the child from the anxiety of the imminent injection. It is not correct to tell the child to be brave since this belittles the feelings expressed by the child. Preschool children have a limited sense of time, so telling the child that the pain will only last a few seconds may not be effective. Restraining the child with other staff should be used last after other methods have failed.

question: A 14-year-old female who has type 1 diabetes mellitus that has been well-controlled for several years is admitted to the hospital for treatment of severe hyperglycemia. The patient's lab values indicate poor glycemic control for the past 3 months. The nurse caring for this patient will suspect which cause for the change in diabetic control?
op_a: Adolescent rebellion and noncompliance
op_b: Changes in cognitive function
op_c: Hormonal fluctuations
op_d: Possible experimentation with drugs or alcohol
exp: In adolescence, hormonal changes and growth spurts may necessitate changes in medication dosages; many children with chronic illness require dosage adjustments in the early teen years.

question: The nurse is teaching a 15-year-old female patient and her parents about an antibiotic the adolescent will begin taking. The drug is known to decrease the effectiveness of oral contraceptive pills (OCPs). The nurse will
op_a: ask the adolescent and her parents whether she is taking OCPs.
op_b: tell her parents privately that pregnancy may occur if she is taking OCPs.
op_c: tell her privately that the medication may decrease the effectiveness of OCPs.
op_d: warn her and her parents that she may get pregnant if she is relying on OCPs.
exp: When soliciting adolescent health histories, the nurse should consider issues related to sexual practices and should provide privacy when asking sensitive questions or giving sensitive information. The other actions do not allow for patient privacy.

question: The nurse is caring for an older adult patient who is receiving multiple medications. When monitoring this patient for potential drug toxicity, the nurse should review which lab values closely?
op_a: Complete blood count and serum glucose levels
op_b: Pancreatic enzymes and urinalysis
op_c: Serum creatinine and liver function tests (LFTs)
op_d: Serum lipids and electrolytes
exp: With liver and kidney dysfunction, the efficacy of drugs is generally increased and may cause toxicity. The nurse should review serum creatinine levels to monitor renal function and LFTs to monitor hepatic function. The other lab tests may be ordered for specific drugs if they affect those body systems.

question: An older patient who reports a 2- to 3-year history of upper gastrointestinal symptoms will begin taking ranitidine (Zantac) to treat this disorder. The patient has completed a health history form. The nurse notes that the patient answered no when asked if any medications were being taken. Which action will the nurse take next?
op_a: Ask whether the patient uses over-the-counter (OTC) medications.
op_b: Obtain a careful dietary history for the past two weeks.
op_c: Recommend that the patient take antacid tablets.
op_d: Suggest that the patient add high-potassium foods to the diet.
exp: Many patients do not think of OTC products as medications and often do not list them when asked about medication use. A patient who takes ranitidine along with an OTC antacid could be duplicating medications. A dietary history is important as well but would not be the most important action in this case. The nurse should not recommend antacid tablets or high-potassium foods.

question: To assist an older, confused patient to adhere to a multidrug regimen, the nurse will provide which recommendation?
op_a: Avoid the use of over-the-counter medications.
op_b: Bring all medications to each clinic visit.
op_c: Review the manufacturer's information insert about each medication.
op_d: Save money by getting each drug at the pharmacy with the lowest price.
exp: Patients who take multiple medications should be advised to bring medications to each clinic visit. Patients may take OTC medications as long as those are included in the list of medications reviewed by the provider. Manufacturer's inserts provide an overwhelming amount of information. Patients should be advised to use only one pharmacy.

question: The nurse is caring for an older patient who is taking 25 mg per day of hydrochlorothiazide. The nurse will closely monitor which lab value in this patient?
op_a: Coagulation studies
op_b: White blood count
op_c: Liver function tests
op_d: Serum potassium
exp: Older patients who take doses of hydrochlorothiazide between 25 to 50 mg/day have increased risk of electrolyte imbalances, so potassium should be monitored closely.

question: The nurse is caring for an 82-year-old patient who takes digoxin to treat chronic atrial fibrillation. When caring for this patient, to monitor for drug side effects, what will the nurse will carefully assess?
op_a: Blood pressure
op_b: Heart rate
op_c: Oxygen saturation
op_d: Respiratory rate
exp: Most of digoxin is eliminated by the kidneys, so a decline in kidney function can cause digoxin accumulation, which can cause bradycardia. Digoxin should not be given to any patient with a pulse less than 60 beats per minute.

question: The nurse is caring for an 80-year-old patient who is taking warfarin (Coumadin). Which action does the nurse understand is important when caring for this patient?
op_a: Encouraging the patient to rise slowly from a sitting position
op_b: Initiating a fall-risk protocol
op_c: Maintaining strict intake and output measures
op_d: Monitoring blood pressure frequently
exp: Patients who take anticoagulants have an increased risk of hemorrhage. Older patients have an increased risk of falls that can lead to bleeding complications. Initiating a fall-risk protocol is important. Warfarin does not affect blood pressure and would not cause orthostatic hypotension. Warfarin does not alter urine output.

question: An 80-year-old patient is being treated for an infection. An order for which type of antibiotic would cause concern for the nurse caring for this patient?
op_a: Aminoglycoside
op_b: Cephalosporin
op_c: Penicillin
op_d: Sulfonamide
exp: Penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, and sulfonamides are normally considered safe for the older adult. Aminoglycosides are excreted in the urine and are not usually prescribed for patients older than 75 years.

question: A 75-year-old patient will be discharged home with a prescription for an opioid analgesic. To help the patient minimize adverse effects, what will the nurse recommend for this patient?
op_a: Sucking on lozenges to moisten oral mucosa
op_b: Taking an antacid with each dose
op_c: Taking the medication on an empty stomach
op_d: Using a stool softener
exp: Opioid analgesics can cause constipation. Stool softeners can help minimize this effect. Opioids do not cause dry mouth. Drug absorption may be decreased with an antacid. Opioid analgesics should be taken with food or milk to decrease gastrointestinal irritation.

question: A 75-year-old patient is readmitted to the hospital to treat recurrent pneumonia. The patient had been discharged home with a prescription for antibiotics 5 days prior. The nurse admitting this patient will take which initial action?
op_a: Ask the patient about over-the-counter drug use.
op_b: Ask the patient how many doses of the antibiotic have been taken.
op_c: Discuss increasing the antibiotic dose with the provider.
op_d: Obtain an order for a creatinine clearance test.
exp: There are many reasons for non-adherence to a drug regimen in an older patient, so if a patient is readmitted, the nurse should first ascertain whether or not the medications have been used. Asking the patient how many doses have been taken will help to assess this. If it is determined that the patient is taking the drug as ordered, the other steps may be taken.

question: The nurse is performing an admission assessment on an 80-year-old patient who has frequent hospital admissions. The patient appears more disoriented and confused than usual. Which action by the nurse is correct?
op_a: Asking about medication doses
op_b: Asking for a neurologist consult
op_c: Requesting orders for liver function tests
op_d: Suspecting impaired renal function
exp: An initial sign of drug toxicity in elderly patients may be confusion or changes in behavior. The nurse should ask about drug doses and notify the provider of the behaviors. The provider may order further evaluation based on examination of the patient.

question: An older patient takes ibuprofen for arthritis pain. The patient tells the nurse that the ibuprofen causes gastrointestinal (GI) upset. Which action will the nurse take with this patient?
op_a: Ask the provider about having the patient take a different medication.
op_b: Instruct the patient to cut the ibuprofen dose in half to avoid GI upset.
op_c: Explain that all drugs have adverse effects.
op_d: Explore options to help decrease the drug side effects.
exp: Older adults are more likely to experience drug side effects, and nurses should be aware of measures that may decrease these side effects and thus improve adherence.

question: The nurse is caring for a 78-year-old patient who lives independently. The patient will begin a new drug regimen that requires taking multiple drugs at various times per day. Which intervention is appropriate for the nurse to implement with this patient?
op_a: Ask the patient's family members to monitor the patient's drug regimen.
op_b: Develop a log to record the times each drug will be taken.
op_c: Reinforce the need to take the drugs as scheduled.
op_d: Write the medication administration times on each prescription label.
exp: The patient should be advised to keep a medication record of drugs and when they will be taken. The patient is independent, and this helps maintain independence. Family member support is essential when older patients are confused. Reinforcing information without providing a means to keep track of the medications does not necessarily improve compliance. Writing medication times on prescription labels does not help to organize the medication schedule.

question: The nurse is preparing an 80-year-old patient for discharge home from the hospital. The patient will receive several new medications. The patient lives alone but has several family members who stop by every day. Which suggestions will the nurse make for this family? (Select all that apply.)
op_a: Ask the pharmacy for non-childproof medication bottles.
op_b: Ask the patient to record all medications and the times they are taken.
op_c: Place the pills in an organizer container.
op_d: Provide the patient with the drug manufacturer information sheets.
op_e: Put water bottles near pills for convenience.
exp: To help older patients with compliance, medications should be convenient and easy to open. Asking the pharmacist for non-childproof containers will help make medications easier to get. Using an organizer container helps patients remember which drugs should be taken at what time. Placing water bottles nearby eliminates a step in the process and increases the likelihood that a medication will be taken on time.

question: Which drug properties are problematic for older patients? (Select all that apply.)
op_a: Drugs with anticholinergic effects
op_b: Drugs that are highly protein-bound
op_c: Drugs with a short half-life
op_d: Drugs that undergo hepatic conjugation
op_e: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic range
exp: Older patients are more susceptible to drug side effects, especially those that cause anticholinergic effects. Older patients have a loss of protein-binder sites for drugs, so those that are highly protein-bound will have higher than usual serum levels and can cause toxicity. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic range require closer monitoring in all patients, but especially in older patients. Drugs with a short half-life are preferred because older patients have a decreased ability to metabolize and excrete drugs. Hepatic conjugation is usually not influenced by older age, liver diseases, or drug interaction.
